paragraphs: Freelance software development cost depends on the workflow, platforms and integrations you need, rather than a universal starting price. I separate development fees from hosting, maps, messaging and other recurring services. Use this checklist to compare the same scope across quotes and send me your requirements by email or WhatsApp.
By Gagan Shukla · 12 Oct 2026 · 5 min read

There is no reliable single price for every app, website or SaaS product. A quote depends on what users must do, how many roles need access, the integrations involved, existing content or data, and the work needed to test and launch it. Gagan Shukla provides a project-specific written quote after reviewing your requirements; this guide does not publish a starting price or imply that every project fits one package.

For a useful comparison, send the same brief to each developer. A cheaper total may exclude design, backend work, deployment, testing or handover that another quote includes. Ask each supplier to list assumptions, exclusions and recurring costs.
Choose one essential end-to-end workflow for the first release. List later features separately so a version-one quote does not silently include your entire long-term roadmap.

Your development contract and your software operating costs are separate decisions. Hosting, domains, SMS, maps, payment-provider charges, email services and app-store accounts may have recurring or usage-based fees. Your business should own the relevant accounts and review the providers’ current charges before approval.

A credible timeline follows the agreed scope. It also depends on the availability of content, design approvals, integration documentation, test accounts and the person accepting each milestone. Store reviews and third-party approvals are external dependencies and should not be promised as fixed dates controlled by the developer.

Break delivery into reviewable milestones: discovery and scope, approved workflows, a working core journey, integration and testing, then launch and handover. Each milestone needs an acceptance checklist, not only a calendar date.

A fixed-scope quote suits a clearly defined website, app release or MVP. A freelance retainer suits ongoing changes when priorities evolve and you want an agreed block of development time. In both cases, document deliverables, review hours, ownership and a process for approving additional work. These are freelance contracts, not employment offers.

Gagan’s relevant portfolio includes VRC Mobility, TruckMitr, HRMS/CRM, bid management and SaaS work. Review the closest project and use the contact page to discuss your requirements. Prior project results are useful context, not guarantees of leads or revenue for a new product.

A logistics application can mean a driver app, truck booking platform, operations dashboard, fleet system or field-agent CRM. Write down the allowed status changes and the person responsible for each one. This helps prevent a driver app and an office dashboard from showing inconsistent operational states. It also makes testing concrete: each role should see and change only what the workflow permits.

Decide which information a driver needs while offline, which actions can be queued and which actions require an immediate server response. A stored form and live vehicle location behave differently when connectivity disappears. The screen should make pending synchronisation visible rather than reporting success too early.

Describe why location is needed and who should see it. Agree on update frequency, battery expectations, foreground and background behaviour, and what the dashboard shows when location is stale. Location permissions and device limitations need to be part of the product design.

For notifications, define the event, recipient and useful next action. An assignment alert should lead to the correct job. A missed update should have a clear follow-up path. Choose provider integrations after the notification requirements are understood.

Avoid promising an integration before checking the available documentation, access and business rules. If you have existing data, list what must be migrated and which records must remain accessible. The first phase can focus on the most useful workflow while later integrations remain separately scoped.

For a first release, choose one driver or staff workflow, the corresponding office view and a clear definition of completion. Include the roles, error states and offline cases in the acceptance criteria. Review the working product at milestones rather than waiting until the final delivery.

By Gagan Shukla · 12 Oct 2026 · 5 min read

When you contact me about freelance development, you do not need a technical specification. Start with the work your business needs to do. Explain who uses the product, what they do today and where the process becomes slow, confusing or expensive. A workflow is more useful than a long list of technologies.

For a website, this might be helping visitors understand your services and enquire. For a CRM, it might be keeping enquiries and follow-ups visible. For a SaaS product, it might be giving customers a repeatable tool they can subscribe to. For a bid management system, it might be keeping opportunities, documents and approvals together.

Describe the smallest version that would be useful to a real user. Separate required launch features from features that can wait. This helps me quote a defined scope and helps you evaluate whether the first release solves the original problem.

Payments, maps, email, accounting software, identity providers and external APIs can materially change the scope. Tell me which tools you already use, whether API documentation is available and who controls those accounts. Avoid sending passwords or customer data in your first enquiry.

If you are replacing an existing tool, describe the records you need to keep and how you can export them. Migration and historical reports should be scoped explicitly. An existing product may also need a code review before a reliable maintenance or feature quote is possible.

A budget range helps us decide what belongs in the first phase. If you do not have one, say so and I can discuss scope options. Mention any fixed launch date and the reason for it. I estimate after understanding the requirements rather than promising one price for every website or application.

I am based in Noida, India, and accept freelance enquiries from any country. Include your country or time zone and preferred written review deadlines. We can agree on a communication window, written updates and demonstrations that fit the project. Payment terms and currency are confirmed before work starts.

My portfolio includes the VRC Mobility website, a bid management system, HRMS and SaaS work, alongside mobile app projects. Use the project and service pages to identify relevant experience, then ask about the requirements that matter for your own product.

By Gagan Shukla · 8 Oct 2026 · 7 min read Start with an off-the-shelf CRM, unless one of these is true Zoho, HubSpot and Salesforce are excellent products. For a small team with a standard sales pipeline, they are usually the right first step. A custom CRM starts to make sense when the tool begins to shape your business instead of the other way around. Signs you have outgrown an off-the-shelf CRM Per-seat licences are growing faster than revenue as you add telecallers, field agents or franchisees. Your team keeps a parallel spreadsheet because the CRM cannot model your process (site visits, quotations, service tickets, dealer networks). Field staff need a simple mobile app that works offline, not a complex desktop dashboard. You need deep integration with your own systems: ERP, billing, inventory, WhatsApp or a customer app. Customer data must be hosted in a specific region or stay fully under your control. What a custom CRM typically includes Lead capture from website forms, ads and calls, with automatic assignment. Custom pipeline stages that match your real sales process. Mobile apps for telecallers and field agents, with call logging and visit check-ins. Role-based access for admins, managers and agents. Automated follow-up reminders via push, email or WhatsApp. Dashboards for conversion, team performance and revenue. I built exactly this kind of system with TMConnect, a Flutter CRM for telecallers and field agents, and an HRMS & CRM app published on both app stores. A quick build-vs-buy checklist Will licence costs over the next 3 years exceed a one-time build plus hosting? Is your sales process a competitive advantage that generic tools flatten? Do you have field or mobile-first users? Do you need to own your data and integrations end to end? Tip: If you answered yes to two or more, a custom CRM, often built in phases starting with the most painful workflow, is worth a written scope review.
